### `libgit2/src/util/utf8.c` integration: the switch from C

The campaign's first switch, run by `modules/libgit2/src/util/utf8.c/integration/run-1` on the
module's branch after the merge of the working branch (`43605086f`): `012d1d34c`, and the
fork's `1b37e3d08`. The export feature `ffi-export-src-util-utf8-c` is deleted, the crate's
only one, so `utf8.rs`'s gateway compiles from now on, and its four `unit_priv` tests run in
`lib`. The module's six `equiv` tests are retired with the C they compared
(`tests/equiv/src/util/utf8.rs`); their cases stay in its unit tests and doctests. The raw
bindings of `git_utf8_iterate`, `git_utf8_char_length` and `git_utf8_valid_buf_length` stay,
and now reach the exports. `src/util/utf8.c` leaves `c/`: the change is the commit
`integrate src/util/utf8.c` on a local `fork/main`, which stands for
`crustify-rs/libgit2-fork`'s `main` and is not pushed, and `.gitmodules` names the fork.
`utf8.h` stays for `path.c`, `diff_xdiff.c` and `fs_path.c`. The module's tied C test,
`tests/util/utf8.c`, calls `git_utf8_char_length` alone, so it stays and checks the export.
No C test leaves, so no case needs listing. The exports are a private module's, so the
crate's API does not change.

The switch also made the one-time change of the C build. The fork's
`cmake/SelectRust.cmake` links the static library that `LIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY` names wherever
the remaining C is linked: `libgit2.so`, the CLI, `libgit2_tests` and `util_tests`. It is an
imported target among `LIBGIT2_SYSTEM_LIBS`. `libgit2.so` keeps the Rust's symbols local
(`--exclude-libs`). Its dynamic symbols are the previous generation's on every variant,
`asan-ubsan`'s two linker-made `__start_`/`__stop_asan_globals` aside. Those come from LLVM
23's instrumentation of the Rust and are protected. Without the variable, the library leaves
the three exports undefined, as the crate's bundled and shared builds of `c/` need. Each
variant's `build` command first makes the library (`crustify/scripts/rust-staticlib.sh`),
between `configure` and the C's link. It builds the crate of the checkout that runs it as a
`staticlib` on the dev profile, the profile the Rust tests run on, so that the C tests check
the same build with debug assertions and overflow checks on. It builds in campaign mode
against the configured variant, with `--features bindgen`, so that the committed bindings
are checked, and with `CRUSTIFY_STATICLIB`, under which `build.rs` reads the build's
configuration and links none of its C. It instruments the Rust as `cargo-variant.sh` does.
`nm` shows that the library defines only the Rust, the three exports and the crate's
`__extern` wrappers, and no libgit2 C. Every other campaign build leaves the library out of
its link, matched by canonical path, so that no binary holds the Rust twice. BSan has no
`cargo bsan rustc`, so a stand-in for the cargo it runs turns its `build` into `rustc
--crate-type staticlib`. The BSan runtime its driver bundles is removed from the copy, since
the variant's C link links it.

The variants were rebuilt as a new generation, `crustify/builds.gen1`, with
`crustify/scripts/build-variants.sh`, and this worktree's `crustify/builds` links to it.
`crustify/builds` itself, which three batches were using, was left untouched. Each variant is
configured from the generation's own `c`, a detached worktree of the fork at `1b37e3d08`, so
that the build outlives this worktree and the base checkout's next moves (`build.json`
version 7). Each archive holds 212 objects, where the previous generation's held 213:
`utf8.c.o` is gone. Each variant passed its smoke test (`util_tests -sutf8`). In every
variant, `utf8proc_utf8class` is absent from the C test executables, which take
`git_utf8_iterate` from the Rust; in `libgit2.so` it is a local symbol.

Gates on `012d1d34c`, over gen1, from `end-gates` snapshots at 24 jobs. The workspace is
formatted, and `clippy --workspace --all-targets` passes with warnings denied. Plain passes
the whole workspace: `lib` 848 and 1 ignored, `equiv` 528, `ub_safe` 763, `ub_unsafe` 120,
`unit_pub` 84, `hidden_symbols` 1, doctests 76 and 378. ASan+UBSan and TSan pass it but for
the known nightly failures: the 9 `compile_fail` snapshots and the `CommitBuilder` doctest
(E0624). Miri passes every binary: `lib` 400, `ub_safe` 194, `equiv` 38, `unit_pub` 49,
`ub_unsafe` 19, the rest marked. The remaining C tests ran over the link with the Rust,
through `crustify/scripts/c-tests.sh`. It runs `build.json`'s `ctest` command, then every
suite alone as the baseline did, and compares the result with `c-baseline.json`. Plain,
ASan+UBSan and TSan give 3443 passed and 55 skipped of 3498, coverage 3444 and 54, each the
baseline's record. Under TSan, the same 10 suites as the baseline's report the C's
lock-order inversions and races, and no case fails; no report has a Rust frame. `ctest`
passes both targets on plain, ASan+UBSan and coverage. Under TSan it fails `offline` on those
reports alone, 49 lock-order inversions and glibc's `tzset` race. BSan was rebuilt and not
run, as the settings' `sanitizers` answer has it. `c/` changed, so the crate was packaged as
`package-gate-procedure` has it. The package has 697 files, `utf8.c` out and
`SelectRust.cmake` in, and builds alone in bundled mode. Its `libgit2.pc`'s
`Requires.private` also needs the side campaigns' installs on `PKG_CONFIG_PATH`, beside
`CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH`. Its `lib` tests link, `path.c`'s `next_hfs_char` calling the Rust export.
790 pass, among them the module's; the other 58 need the fixture repositories of
`c/tests/resources`, which the package leaves out.

From the switch on, the module's coverage is its Rust's: `utf8.c` is in no build, and the C
figures lose its 71 lines. This run did not measure coverage. The procedure this switch
worked out, which every later switch repeats, is proposed for the spec
(`crustify/evolution/module-switch-procedure`). That libgit2's switch removes a file and no
CMake line is a lesson. Usage cells are the assistant's.

### `libgit2/deps/ntlmclient/compat.h` wave 200 batch 0: `MIN`

`deps/ntlmclient/compat.h` is a header with no translation unit, and its one scheduled item is
`#define MIN(x, y) (((x) < (y)) ? (x) : (y))`, under `#ifndef MIN`; the header's `bool`,
`true` and `false` are defined only under `_MSC_VER`. `mac::MIN` is the native
`fn min<T: PartialOrd>(x: T, y: T) -> T` in `src/libgit2/deps/ntlmclient/compat_h.rs`, the
macro's body over any `PartialOrd` type: ties and pairs `<` cannot order return `y`, as the C
does, and for an `Ord` type the result is `core::cmp::min`'s, the plan's `rust_equivalent`. It
is not a `const fn`, since a generic comparison cannot be called in a constant on stable Rust
1.100. Its docs name where it departs from the macro: one operand type rather than the usual
arithmetic conversions, and each operand evaluated once, where the macro evaluates the one

#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
    # crustify/scripts/coverage/ measures the suites as the testing spec's Coverage section does.
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/profraw/%p-%m.profraw}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  asan-ubsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address"
    export ASAN_OPTIONS=${ASAN_OPTIONS:-detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1}
    export UBSAN_OPTIONS=${UBSAN_OPTIONS:-print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  tsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    # glibc's tzset locks what TSan cannot see: see tsan.supp.
    export TSAN_OPTIONS=${TSAN_OPTIONS:-halt_on_error=1:suppressions=$here/crustify/scripts/tsan.supp}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" -Zbuild-std --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  bsan)
    # trybuild's nested cargo build does not finish under BorrowSanitizer, and the
    # compile-fail suite is a compile-time check the plain variant already runs.
    # Under parallel test threads BorrowSanitizer's GC can take longer than its default
    # 10 s hang threshold to bring every thread to a safepoint, and then aborts; give it
    # 120 s rather than serialize the tests.
    export BSAN_OPTIONS=${BSAN_OPTIONS:-gc_hang_threshold_ms=120000}
    if [ "${1:-}" = test ]; then
      case " $* " in
        *" -- "*) exec cargo bsan "$@" --skip compile_fail ;;
        *) exec cargo bsan "$@" -- --skip compile_fail ;;
      esac
    fi
    exec cargo bsan "$@" ;;
  *)
    echo "unknown variant: $variant" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

# The packaging gate's command is worked out by hand

Status: `open`.

## Signal

A procedure I had to work out by hand, over three failed runs, that the gate names but does
not give.

## Evidence

`wave-186/batch-0/run-1` changed the raw bindings (`sys/git2/allowlist.txt`). Per
`testing-gates`' Regressions section, that means it packages the safe crate "built alone in
bundled mode … each crate the package depends on … patched to its local source". Run from
the worktree with `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=` and `--allow-dirty`:

1. `cargo package` failed: `no matching package named glibc-bindings found` (crates.io). The
   manifest's `[patch."https://github.com/crustify-rs/…"]` does not apply to the packaged
   manifest, whose dependencies are registry ones. The fix was
   `--config 'patch.crates-io.glibc-bindings.path="/target/glibc-crustify"'
   --config 'patch.crates-io.ffibox.path="/crustify-rs/ffibox"'`.
2. The bundled CMake configure then failed: `PCRE2 support was requested but not found`, and
   after that `system zlib was requested but not found`. The side campaigns' installs
   (`<repo>/../{openssl,pcre2,zlib}-bindings/crustify/builds/plain/install`) have to be on
   `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH`, and colon-separated, since that is the environment variable's form.
   The `plain` variant's `configure` in `build.json` passes them semicolon-separated, as a
   `-D` value, and copying that form failed.

With both changes, the crate packaged 698 files and verified.

## Destination

A campaign artifact the assistant owns: a script beside `crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh`
(such as `crustify/scripts/package.sh`) that runs the gate with the patches derived from the
manifest's `[patch]` sections and the side installs from `build.json`'s `plain` prefix path.
Its use would then go in `testing-gates`' Regressions section, or in a lesson until the
wrappers are published.

## Change

Not made: neither file is the translator's. The command that passed:

```bash
S=$(realpath -m crustify/builds/plain/../../../..)
I() { echo "$S/$1-bindings/crustify/builds/plain/install"; }
CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT= OPENSSL_ROOT_DIR=$(I openssl) \
CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$(I openssl):$(I pcre2):$(I zlib)" \
PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$(I pcre2)/lib/pkgconfig:$(I zlib)/lib/pkgconfig" \
cargo package --allow-dirty \
  --config 'patch.crates-io.glibc-bindings.path="/target/glibc-crustify"' \
  --config 'patch.crates-io.ffibox.path="/crustify-rs/ffibox"'
```

## Validation

The command above packaged and verified the tree of `wave-186/batch-0`. The two earlier
forms failed as quoted.

## Review

None yet.

content.content: --- name: ffibox description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one." --- # ffibox ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a value; what C does not alias is plain Rust. Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md` describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes. What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there. ## Planning ### Dependencies › Adopted crates A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists, each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses. ## Binding workflow ### Binding workflow › Rust tree The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory. ## Binding and porting Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`, `docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too. ### Binding types A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them. ### Binding types › Safe layout While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox;`, and `CArc` for `FooArc`. A value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal`. ### Binding symbols › Functions A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them. ### Binding symbols › Function pointers A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier, `callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body. A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a `CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as `docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table. ### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C. ### Porting › FFI boundary An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does with the Rust it reaches: - the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`, `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return its owners and handles; - memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C frees it through an exported release; - a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a `CPayload`; and - the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`. ### Porting types › Structs Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as [Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its `port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox`, its handles unchanged, until its `port/layout` makes it `Box`, or `Pin>` while C keeps its address. Between a struct's `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, its layout is native while C still allocates or frees its storage, and ffibox's single-object owners, which hold only C-layout types, cannot hold it. Where C releases it with its allocation family's free alone, and the native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop (`size_of::() != 0` and `!core::mem::needs_drop::()`, both asserted at compile time), and C does not keep its address, `FooBox` is `Box>` and a counted run of them `Vec>`, `P` the family's `Copy` policy with the alignment the family guarantees: an existing `CLenAlloc` policy of the family, or one declared with `impl_clenalloc!`'s `align =`. A box is built with `CAllocator::try_box`, which refuses an over-aligned type at compile time and returns C's out-of-memory failure, and handed to C with `Box::into_raw_with_allocator`; a run grows with `Vec::try_reserve`, keeping C's out-of-memory failure, and is handed to C through `CVec::try_from` and `into_raw_parts`. A pointer C hands back is adopted with `Box::from_raw_in`, under the conditions `CBox::into_box`'s documentation lists, and a run with `Vec::from_raw_parts_in`, its length as its capacity, under the allocator's fit rule. Its `port/memory` makes them `Box` and `Vec`. ## Testing ### Testing › UB tests The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test. ## Reviewing Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`. ### Reviewing › Objectives A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. Under `ub`, the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists are the checklist: each is excluded by the primitive or the producer's contract it names, or is a finding. ### Reviewing › Reports A soundness or ergonomics gap in ffibox itself, in its safe primitives or its unsafe FFI seams, is a defect in a tool: a proposal, as any tool defect is.

# ffibox

Generic smart pointers and traits for building safe Rust wrappers over C
types and pointers, in both directions: memory C owns, held from Rust, and
memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Designed for arbitrary
user-space C interop, including the case where you need direct field access
and a C-ABI-compatible layout (porting C internals to Rust in place), not just
opaque-handle wrapping.

## Why

Wrapping a C API in Rust means re-homing C's ownership and lifecycle
conventions into RAII. The recurring shapes:

- A C-allocated object with a destructor (`free`), and maybe a copy (`dup`).
- A constructor or allocator (`foo_alloc`, `malloc`, `calloc`) whose result
  must be released by its paired free.
- A refcounted object shared by several holders (`up_ref` / `unref`), maybe
  with a C lock over the state they mutate.
- Types with multiple or runtime-conditional destructors.
- A by-value struct whose teardown disposes its fields but not the struct.
- An owned length-aware buffer or NUL-terminated `char *` with a C destructor.
- A type-erased `void *` that stays opaque end to end.

Each shape gets one owner type, generic over a **policy** — a type you declare
that names the C routines. `impl_cdrop!` and its siblings bind a C routine to a
policy; a type alias names the pair: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`.

## Mental model in one paragraph

No reference to C-owned memory is formed while anything may write or free it:
objects are reached through handles, and only a run of bytes nothing writes
while it is lent is a `&CStr` or `&[u8]`. Each C type gets a layout type
`Foo` (`#[repr(transparent)]` over `ffi::foo`; `Foo<'r>` when the C object
borrows its parent) and two borrowed handles, `FooRef<'a>` / `FooMut<'a>`,
each one pointer wide and carrying the getters and setters; field access projects a raw pointer out of the handle. Ownership
comes in three shapes: `CBox<Foo, P>` is the sole owner of an object behind a
pointer and releases it through the policy `P`; `CArc<Foo, P>` is one of
several counted references and hands out the shared handle, the exclusive one
only when the count proves it sole, and — for an object with a C lock — a
`CGuard` whose `FooLocked<'a>` handle reaches the state that lock protects; and
`CVal<Foo, P>` holds the object inline and disposes its resources on drop.
A policy that also constructs gives `CBox` and `CArc` safe constructors that
allocate through it, so a safely built owner is always freed by the routine
paired with its allocator.
Strings, buffers and borrowed runs get their own types; a buffer drops its
elements, so a `foo **` of owned objects releases each one.

The other direction uses the same terms. `RustAlloc` is the policy over Rust's
allocator, so an object Rust allocates is held as one C allocated, and
`CAllocator` is a C allocation family as the standard `Allocator`, so a
`Box` or `Vec` holds memory C frees; `CClosure`
and `CPayload` put a Rust closure behind a C function pointer and its
context, for one call or until C releases it; `CFn` and `CFnBox` hold a C
function and its context that Rust calls, and `CCallback` and `CCallbackBox`
either half; `CTable` holds Rust state behind a C table of function
pointers C calls into, its slots minted by `impl_cvtable!` from a trait the
Rust side implements; the `export_*!` macros offer a policy to C as the
routine it calls, with the owner and handle types in its signature.
[docs/ownership.md](docs/ownership.md) lists the owners and the policies;
[docs/borrows.md](docs/borrows.md) lists the handles. Each walks from a C
declaration to the type it wants.

## Install

```toml
[dependencies]
ffibox = "0.1"
```

ffibox needs Rust 1.100 or later (`rust-version` in `Cargo.toml`), the first
release with the standard `Allocator` interface, which `CAllocator` implements
over a C allocation family.

ffibox is `#![no_std]`. The `std` feature (on by default) selects
`std::process::abort` for the unrecoverable-failure path (`Clone` or
`make_mut` when the C copy or up_ref fails), where without it that path is a
double-panic, and lets `CClosure`, `CTable`'s slots and `callback::barrier`
catch a panic before it reaches C. The `alloc` feature, which `std` enables,
adds `RustAlloc`, `CPayload`, `CCallbackBox` and `CTable`, which allocate
through Rust's global allocator, and the conversions between ffibox's owners
and `Box` / `Vec`; nothing else allocates but through a policy the consumer
chose, as `CAllocator` allocates through its family.

```toml
[dependencies]
ffibox = { version = "0.1", default-features = false }
```

## Documentation

Every wrapper answers one question first: **does dropping the Rust value
release the object?** This is about who *releases* the object, not who
allocated it — a `CBox` usually points at memory C allocated.

- **Yes** — it is owned → [docs/ownership.md](docs/ownership.md)
- **No** — C, or a parent object, releases it → [docs/borrows.md](docs/borrows.md)

When it is Rust's memory that C holds, calls or reads →
[docs/outbound.md](docs/outbound.md).

| doc | what is in it |
|-----|---------------|
| [goals.md](docs/goals.md) | what the primitives aim for, in both directions, and how each aim is checked |
| [examples.md](docs/examples.md) | eight self-contained wrappers, each compiled as a doctest |
| [ownership.md](docs/ownership.md) | `CBox`, `CBoxState`, `CVal`, `CStrBox`, `CVec`, `CArc`; the lifecycle policies; picking an owner and a policy; `Box` and `Vec` over a C allocator (`CAllocator`) |
| [borrows.md](docs/borrows.md) | `Foo`, `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooLocked`, `CGuard`, `CGuardedRef`, `CSlice`, `CSliceMut`, `CNullTerminated`; where the accessors live; the seam traits |
| [outbound.md](docs/outbound.md) | Rust's side: `RustAlloc`, the callbacks (`CClosure`, `CPayload`, `CFn`, `CFnBox`, `CCallback`, `CCallbackBox`), C tables (`CTable`), out-parameters, the panic barrier, the `export_*!` macros |
| [vtables.md](docs/vtables.md) | C tables of function pointers implemented in Rust: `CTable`, `impl_cvtable!`, their receivers, re-entry, panics and release, and the design |
| [patterns.md](docs/patterns.md) | C's iteration, error and callback conventions as Rust's iterators, `Result` and closures |
| [hand-written.md](docs/hand-written.md) | the wrappers `define_ctype!` cannot express (a layout type generic over a type), and the owners no policy expresses |

Upgrading? [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) says what each release changes, and
how to migrate code that still compiles but behaves differently.

# Outbound Outbound is Rust's side of the boundary: memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. The inbound documents, [ownership.md](ownership.md) and [borrows.md](borrows.md), cover memory C owns held from Rust; this one walks the other way, with the same terms. ffibox is needed only where C **aliases** a value: keeps a pointer to it after a call returns, frees it, or calls back into it. A pointer passed down for one call and not kept is plain Rust: `&mut x as *mut _` for C that writes, `&x as *const _` for C that only reads, a `&CStr` or a slice's `as_ptr()`. ## The primitives | C does | Primitive | Rust counterpart | |--------|-----------|------------------| | frees an object or buffer Rust allocated | an owner under `RustAlloc`, surrendered with `into_raw` / `into_c` | `Box::into_raw` | | frees a string or buffer with its own allocator | `CStrBox::from_c_str`, `CVec::from_slice`, `CVec::from_fn`, `CVec::new_uninit` under that allocator's policy | `CString`, `Vec` | | frees a value or buffer Rust built, and grew, in C's allocator | `Box>` / `Vec>`, into a `CBox` / `CVec` and surrendered with `into_c` / `into_raw_parts` | `Box::new_in`, `Vec::new_in` | | calls a closure during one call | `CClosure`: `ctx()` and `trampoline()` | `&mut F` | | keeps a closure or value, and releases it later | `CPayload`: `into_raw()`, `release_fn()`, `trampoline()` | `Box` | | hands Rust a function and its context to call | `CFn` for the call or borrow it came with, `CFnBox` with the routine that releases the context: `call()`, `parts()` / `into_raw()` | a closure | | holds a callback that is either a Rust closure or a C function | `CCallback` (for a call or borrow), `CCallbackBox` (kept until released): `call()` from Rust, `c_form()` / `into_c()` to C | `impl FnMut`, `Box` | | calls into a table of function pointers, each slot passed the table (a backend, a stream) | `CTable`, its slots from `impl_cvtable!`: `as_c_ptr()` / `into_c()`, released through its `release` slot | `Box` | | returns an object through an out-parameter | `CBox::from_c_out`, `CStrBox::from_raw_out` | a return value | | calls a Rust routine that must not unwind into it | `callback::barrier` | `catch_unwind` | | frees, copies or constructs a ported type's objects | `export_cdrop!`, `export_cdupclone!`, `export_cnew!` | the C routines they replace | ## Choosing a primitive - **C frees it.** The memory comes from the allocator C frees with. If that is C's own (`free`, `lib_free`), build it through that allocator's policy: `CVec::from_fn` and `CVec::new_uninit` with a `CLenAlloc` policy, `CVec::from_slice` and `CStrBox::from_c_str` with a copying one, or a `Box` / `Vec` over `CAllocator

` when Rust builds or grows it natively, converted into a `CBox` / `CVec` to hand over. If C frees it through a Rust routine, allocate with `RustAlloc` and offer the release with `export_cdrop!`. Then surrender it with `into_raw`. - **C calls back during the call** (`foreach`, `qsort_r`). `CClosure::new` over `&mut F`. The trampoline's type is inferred from the C declaration it is passed to, and the closure's arguments are the C types, which the binding converts to handles before calling its consumer's closure. With `std`, a panic stops the C routine through the failure value and resumes after it, at `finish()`; a re-entrant invocation is refused the same way. `F: Send` unless the routine calls back on the calling thread only (`unsafe CClosure::new_local`). - **C keeps the callback** (`set_log_callback(cb, ctx, free)`). `CPayload` over an `Fn` closure, surrendered with `into_raw`, released by C through `release_fn()`. C may call it from several threads or re-entrantly, so it is reached as `&F`, and `into_raw` requires `Send + Sync`; state it changes goes behind a `Mutex` or an atomic. A panic in it aborts, so a fallible body goes in `barrier`. - **C keeps a value** (a container's payload, user data). `CPayload`, and `CPayload::borrow` inside the callbacks that receive it. - **C hands Rust a callback** (an options struct's `progress_cb` and `payload`, a ported function's `cb, ctx` arguments through its export). `CFn::new`, `unsafe`, states what the C that supplies the pair guarantees; `call((args…))` takes C's argument types, the context left out, so the binding's safe callable converts its arguments and calls in one justified block. `parts()` hands the pair to another C routine unchanged, with no trampoline between. - **A callable is either** (a field a consumer sets with a closure and C sets with a function, a callback ported code calls whoever supplied it). `CCallback` / `CCallbackBox` hold whichever it is: called from Rust, a closure runs through its trampoline, with the same refusal and panic handling as when C calls it, and handed to C, a C function goes as its own pair. - **C calls into a table Rust implements** (`git_config_backend`, a `git_writestream`: a struct of function pointers, each passed the table). `CTable`, the state `S` behind the table of the layout type `T`, whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints from the trait `S` implements: each slot declares its receiver, `&S` or `&mut S`, which decides what re-entry it allows, and its results for a panic and a refusal. C releases it through the slot declared `release`. [vtables.md](vtables.md) walks through it. A caller that keeps the bytes past the object's borrow takes an owned copy; - a NULL-terminated array of pointers → `CNullTerminated<'a, T>`, an `Iterator` of the elements' borrows; a `count` + `get(i)` pair or a `->next` chain is `(0..n).map(get)` or `iter::successors` over the safe getter; - an object every access reaches under one lock covering all of it — typically a C global and the C lock protecting it → `CGuardedRef<'a, Foo>`, `'static` for a global, with `impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)`; - a NUL string → `&CStr` / `&str` / `&[u8]` tied to the owner's borrow, on the terms of a counted byte run above; - an out-parameter slot → `&'a mut MaybeUninit` from `ptr.cast::>().as_mut()`; no ffibox type; - a `void *` → if it is really a `ffi::foo`, erase a `FooRef` with `as_void_ptr` and recover it with `from_void_ptr` (generically, `T::ref_from_void_ptr` / `T::mut_from_void_ptr` for `T: CCell`); if it is a cookie never looked inside, pass the raw `*mut c_void` through unchanged. A borrow that must outlive its parent's scope (stored next to the parent, sent to a thread) cannot be expressed as a lifetime; copy the child into an owned object instead.

# Hand-written wrappers Only a wrapper `define_ctype!` cannot express — a layout type generic over a type — needs this layer, and so does an owner no policy expresses: [an array freed by one routine](#an-array-freed-by-one-routine) that does more than free its elements and itself. A layout type that carries only lifetimes is not hand-written: `define_ctype!` declares it, `define_ctype!(Blob<'r>, BlobRef, BlobMut, ffi::blob, phantom = &'r Repo)`, as [examples.md](examples.md#a-layout-type-with-a-lifetime--define_ctype-with-phantom) shows. One already written by hand is the same layout, and moves to the macro when its module is next touched, or stays. A C table a library calls into and Rust implements (a backend, a stream: a struct of function pointers, each passed the table) is not hand-written either: `CTable` lays it out with its state, recovers the state in each slot, guards re-entry, puts each slot behind the panic barrier and releases it once, and `impl_cvtable!` mints the slots, as [vtables.md](vtables.md) describes. Only a slot the macro cannot express is written by hand, as an `unsafe extern "C" fn` whose body is `CTable::enter`, in a hand-written `CSlots` impl beside an `unsafe impl CVtable`. What is hand-written for such a wrapper is the layout type, its handles and their seams, against the items below. Its policies are not, unless no macro takes them: - **A layout type generic over a type** (`Stack`) has no elided form, so each of its policies is an `unsafe impl` by hand. - **A hand-written layout type with a lifetime** takes every policy macro, as a `define_ctype!` one does: `impl_cdrop!(BlobFree, Blob<'_>, ffi::blob_free)` implements `CDrop>` for every `'r`, and `impl_cdupclone!` and `impl_cguarded!` name the lifetime, `<'r> BlobFree, Blob<'r>`, as [ownership.md](ownership.md#policies--what-teardown-means) explains. - **A routine of another shape** (a slot, an out-parameter, extra arguments) is no reason to hand-write a policy: a private `unsafe fn` adapter passed to the macro gives it the shape the macro calls, as [ownership.md](ownership.md#policies--what-teardown-means) describes. | Item | Role | Source | |------|------|--------| | `CCell` | the linking trait: `type C` (the FFI type), `type Ref<'a>`, `type Mut<'a>`, and the provided, `unsafe` inbound seam (`ref_from_ptr`, `mut_from_ptr` and their `void *` twins). Its `unsafe impl` promises that `Self` is layout-compatible with `C`, and that `Ref` / `Mut` are `#[repr(transparent)]` over `CBorrowedPtr<'a, Self>` with no `Drop`, and `Mut` invariant in `Self` (a `PhantomData<&'a mut Self>` field) — ffibox builds handles from that layout, and checks their size at compile time. | `src/traits.rs` | | `CRefSeam` / `CMutSeam` / `CLockedSeam` | the handles' seams, every method provided from the layout `CCell` (or `CGuarded`) guarantees: implement them on hand-written handles with `type Cell = Foo;`, as the macros do, or the handles have no `as_ptr` / `as_mut_ptr`. | `src/traits.rs` | | `CBorrowedPtr<'a, T>` | what every handle wraps: one pointer tagged with the borrow's lifetime, `Copy` and covariant like `&'a T`. | `src/refs.rs` | | `CPlainElem` | marker for plain-data elements: every bit pattern is a valid value and there is no C-side identity. It admits `&[T]` from a `CVec`, as a `CSliceElem` (a wrapped C type implements `CCell` instead, so `&[Foo]` does not typecheck), and makes copies read out of memory C keeps writing sound. Not the same as initialized: an unfilled buffer is `CVec, _>` until `assume_init`. | `src/traits.rs` | | `CSliceElem` | elements a `CVec` hands out as `&[T]` / `&mut [T]`: every `CPlainElem`, and the owners — `CBox`, `CArc` and `CStrBox`, bare or in an `Option`, and `CVal` — whose references cover a Rust value, never C memory. A hand-written owner implements it on the same terms. | `src/traits.rs` | **Layout.** `CBox`, `CArc` and `CStrBox` are `#[repr(transparent)]` over their pointer, and their policy is stateless, held in no bytes: `Option>` is a `ffi::foo *`, NULL for `None`, as Rust guarantees for `Option>`. So it takes a raw pointer's place in a `#[repr(C)]` struct, a `foo **` buffer and an `extern "C"` signature alike. A policy with state fails to build in them; it is held by `CBoxState`, `#[repr(C)]` over `{ptr, policy}`, which crosses as a raw pointer. `CVal` is the size of `Foo` under a stateless policy; a buffer is pointer + length, the pointer NULL when empty, as C's `{ T *ptr; size_t len; }`. ## An array freed by one routine A `CVec` releases an array of owners element by element, then frees the buffer through `CLenDrop`, which frees the buffer only (see [ownership.md](ownership.md#choosing-an-owner-what-shape-is-the-owned-thing)). That covers a C routine whose body is only those frees. One that does more — takes a lock, updates a count, or releases an element other than by freeing it — is not a policy: the wrapper writes the owner itself, as `CVec` is written: - private fields, the pointer and the length, adopted by an `unsafe` constructor whose contract is the routine's: the array is one the routine frees, and its non-null elements are distinct allocations it owns; - a `Drop` that calls the routine once, with both; - the elements handed out as borrows tied to `&self` — `FooRef<'_>` through `CRefSeam::from_ptr`, `&CStr`, a `CSlice` of the pointers, which copies them out — never as `&mut` to a slot, through which safe code would store a pointer, or NULL, that the routine then frees. # Ownership An owner is a Rust value whose drop releases a C object. Which owner you reach for follows from the shape of the thing owned; *what* its drop does is a separate choice, the [policy](#policies--what-teardown-means), and the owner's type carries both. For the borrowed side — handles over objects C or a parent releases — see [borrows.md](borrows.md). ## The owners | Scope | Type | From | Role | |-------|------|------|------| | owners | `CBox` | ffibox | the sole owner of an object behind a pointer, released by `P` on drop; `Clone` when `P` deep-copies; built safely by `new` / `new_zeroed` / `new_uninit` when `P` constructs | | | `CBoxState` | ffibox | `CBox` under a policy with state (an allocator context, an element-free callback), stored beside the pointer; crosses to C as a raw pointer | | | `CVal` | ffibox | an owned value held inline, its resources disposed by `P` on drop | | | `CStrBox

` | ffibox | an owned NUL-terminated `char *`; read-only `CStr` / `str` / byte views | | | `CVec` | ffibox | an owned `(ptr, len)` array, NULL when empty; drops its elements, then frees the buffer; `&[T]` for plain elements and owners, `CSlice` for wrapped C objects; `from_fn` / `new_uninit` build one in `P`'s allocator, `from_slice` copies a Rust slice into it | | shared owner | `CArc` | ffibox | one counted reference to a refcounted object; `Clone` through the up_ref; the shared handle always, `get_mut` / `make_mut` when the count proves it sole or after a copy, and `lock()` → `CGuard` when `Foo` is `CGuarded` over part of it | | standard owners over a C allocator | `Box>`, `Vec>` | std, over ffibox's `CAllocator` | a value or buffer Rust owns natively in storage C allocates or frees with the family `P` (`malloc` / `realloc` / `free`); to and from `CBox` / `CVec` over the same `CAllocator

` without copying — see [`Box` and `Vec` over a C allocator](#box-and-vec-over-a-c-allocator) | ## Conventions - **Adopting a pointer is `unsafe`; giving one out is not — as on `Box`.** `from_raw*` / `from_c*` are `unsafe`, since they assert ownership of what the pointer addresses; `into_raw*` / `into_c` and `as_ptr` / `as_c_ptr` are safe, since a raw pointer asserts nothing until someone dereferences it. The owners' `from_raw` / `into_raw` / `as_ptr` speak the Rust-side pointee; `from_c` / `into_c` / `as_c_ptr` on `CBox`, `CBoxState` and `CArc` speak the C type, so C interop is cast-free. The handles have seams of their own — see [borrows.md](borrows.md#conventions). - **The owners behave like their std counterparts where ownership allows.** `CStrBox` derefs to `CStr` and compares and hashes by content, as `CString` does, and converts into one; a `CVec` of plain data or owners derefs to a slice and compares element-wise, as `Vec` does. A `CVec` of C objects does not deref: its elements are reached through handles. - **Constructing through the policy is safe.** `new`, `new_zeroed` and `new_uninit` (each with a `_with(policy)` form) allocate through the routine the owner frees with, and return `None` when C fails, as `from_raw` does on NULL. The one `unsafe` step is `assume_init`, which promotes storage C has filled through `as_c_ptr`. There is no safe `write(value)`: a C object is initialised where it lives. - **`from_raw*` adopts ownership; `from_ptr*` borrows.** Pick the verb by what you return. - **Thread safety is opt-in for wrapped C types, opt-out for raw memory.** `Foo` carries a zero-sized marker withholding `Send` / `Sync`; `CBox`, `CVal`, `CVec` and the views over a `Foo` inherit them once the wrapper writes `unsafe impl Send / Sync for Foo` with a safety proof, on the terms of their std counterparts — `CBox` like `Box`, `CArc` with `Foo: Send + Sync` like `Arc`, and `CGuardedRef` with `Foo: Send` like `&Mutex<_>`. Owners that never name a `Foo` — `CStrBox` and a `CVec` of plain elements (`CVec`) — follow their policy alone, and a unit-struct policy is `Send + Sync`, so **they cross threads by default**. That is right for an allocator any thread may free into (`free`, a library's `lib_free`); for one that must free on the allocating thread, opt out by giving the policy a `PhantomData<*const ()>` field. ## Choosing an owner: what shape is the owned thing? Reached once dropping the Rust value is what releases the object. When it is not, the answer is a borrow instead — see [borrows.md](borrows.md#choosing-a-borrow). - **A NUL-terminated string** (`char *`, no stored length) → `CStrBox

`. `strlen` recovers the length, so one `CDrop` policy covers a plain free and a clearing free alike. Its views are read-only, like `CStr`. - **A counted array** → `CVec`, one policy per allocator family. Plain elements (`CPlainElem`: integers, floats, raw pointers, `MaybeUninit`) and owners (`CSliceElem`) read out as a real `&[T]` because the buffer is exclusively owned; wrapped C objects come out as handles through `as_handles` → `CSlice`, since `&[Foo]` would cover them. Where C returns NULL with 0 for an empty array, adopt with `from_raw_parts_or_empty`; plain `from_raw_parts` treats every NULL as failure. Dropping a `CVec` drops its elements, as a `Vec` does, so the element type says what each slot owns. A wrapper around a `CVec` therefore never drops the elements itself: a `Drop` that does frees each one twice. Up to ffibox 0.1.1 a `CVec` freed the buffer alone, and code written for that is migrated as the [CHANGELOG](../CHANGELOG.md) describes. | C array | element type | |---------|--------------| | `foo **`, each entry owned, NULL allowed | `Option>` | | `char **`, each string owned | `Option>` | | `foo *`, each inline value disposed | `CVal` | | freed with its elements by one routine (`foo_array_free(arr, n)`) | an owner from the rows above, under the array allocator's policy, not that routine | | entries borrowed from elsewhere | the bare pointer | The element type releases the elements, and the policy the array alone: `CLenDrop::c_drop_len` frees the buffer after the `CVec` has dropped every element. So a routine that frees both is never the `CLenDrop`. Over owner elements it frees each a second time; over bare pointers, which are `CPlainElem`, the `CVec` derefs to `&mut [*mut foo]`, through which safe code stores any pointer, or NULL, in a slot the routine then frees; and the policy, a public type, also frees the buffer of a `CVec` of any other element type, whose bytes the routine would read as `foo *`s. Where the routine's body is only those frees, as libgit2's `git_strlist_free` is (`git__free` on each string, then on the array), a `CVec>, GitFree>` releases the same way on drop and the routine is not called. Where it does more, the wrapper is hand-written — see [hand-written.md](hand-written.md#an-array-freed-by-one-routine). Adopting a buffer of owners (`from_raw_parts` and its siblings) asserts that each non-null element is an allocation of its own: a pointer repeated in two slots is freed twice. - **One object held inline** — a local, a field, an array element, with no pointer of its own: - owns no resources → the `Foo` itself (`Foo::zeroed()` when it is `CZeroable`, or a wrapper constructor that has C fill a local); - owns resources and stands alone → `CVal`; - embedded in a parent C struct → a bare `Foo`, disposed by the parent's teardown (a `Drop` on it would dispose twice); - address-sensitive (points into itself, or C recorded its address) → not inline at all: behind a pointer, as below. - **One object behind a pointer** → `CBox` if this is the only reference, `CArc` if it is one of several counted ones. `CBox` owns only `CCell` layout types, from `define_ctype!` or written by hand, as does `CArc`: a `void *` payload is bytes (`CVec`) or a typed owner of its own. ## Policies — what teardown means Every owner's destructor is a **policy**: a type you declare, usually a unit struct deriving `Clone, Copy, Debug, Default`, implementing the lifecycle traits. Bind a C routine to it with the `impl_*!` macros, or implement the traits by hand when teardown needs runtime state. A unit struct is `Send + Sync`, which makes a `CStrBox` or plain-element `CVec` under it free on whichever thread drops it; a thread-bound allocator's policy carries `PhantomData<*const ()>` instead (see [Thread safety](#conventions) above). | Trait | Defines | Macro | Drives | |-------|---------|-------|--------| | `CDrop` | `c_drop` — a `*_free`, or a refcount down-ref | `impl_cdrop!(P, Foo, f)`; `_str` for `c_char` | `CBox`, `CStrBox`, `CArc` | | `CDupClone: CDrop` | `c_dup` — a deep copy (a NEW pointer, NULL on failure) | `impl_cdupclone!(P, Foo, f)`; `_str` for `strdup` | `Clone` / `try_clone` | | `CRefClone: CDrop` | `c_up_ref` — a refcount increment on the SAME pointer; `c_is_sole_owner` (default `false`) | `impl_crefclone!(P, Foo, f)`; `…, ok = |r| r == 1`, `…, sole = g` | `CArc`'s `Clone`, `get_mut`, `make_mut` | | `CLenDrop` | `c_drop_len` — a buffer free, given the byte length; the buffer only, never its elements | `impl_clendrop!(P, f)` | `CVec` | | `CLenClone: CLenDrop` | `c_clone_len` — a buffer memdup (`T: Copy` only) from any readable source; `ALIGN` (default 1) bounds the element types it can copy | `impl_clenclone!(P, f)`, `impl_clenclone!(P, f, align = 16)` | `CVec`'s `Clone`, `CVec::from_slice`, `CSlice::to_cvec` | | `CLenAlloc: CLenDrop` | `c_alloc_len` — uninitialised buffer storage (`malloc(n)`); `ALIGN` as above; `c_realloc_len` — `realloc`, provided as `malloc`, copy and `free` | `impl_clenalloc!(P, f)`, `…, align = 16`, `…, realloc = g` | `CVec::from_fn`, `CVec::new_uninit`, `CAllocator

` | | `CDispose` | `c_dispose` — `*_uninit` / `*_clear` on a value | `impl_cdispose!(P, Foo, f)` | `CVal` | | `CNew: CDrop` | `c_new` — a zero-argument `*_alloc` / `*_new` | by hand | `CBox::new`, `CArc::new` | | `CAlloc: CDrop + CDrop>` | `c_alloc` — uninitialised storage (`malloc`); the free must not read it | by hand | `CBox::new_uninit` | | `CAllocZeroed: CDrop` | `c_alloc_zeroed` — zero-filled storage (`calloc`) | by hand | `CBox::new_zeroed`, `CArc::new_zeroed` | | `CZeroable`, on `Foo` | all-zero is valid for every accessor, safe wrapper and paired teardown; provides `Foo::zeroed()` | `unsafe impl CZeroable for Foo {}` | `new_zeroed`, `Foo::zeroed()` | | `CGuarded`, on `Foo` | `c_lock` / `c_unlock`; the `Locked` handle; the `Scope` it covers | `impl_cguarded!(Foo, FooLocked, lock = f, unlock = g)`; `…, ok = |r| r == 1`; `impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)` for `CGuardedAll` | `CArc::lock`, `CGuardedRef::lock` | `Foo` in the Macro column is any `CCell` layout type, `define_ctype!`'s or hand-written; one that carries a lifetime is written `Foo<'_>`, as **A layout type with a lifetime** below describes, in every macro but `impl_cdupclone!` and `impl_cguarded!`, which name it in a leading list: `<'r> P, Foo<'r>`. **Because the policy is a type parameter, an owner cannot exist without a destructor, and one C type can have several.** `CBox` next to `CBox`: exactly one ever runs per box, chosen by its type. And since each clone trait sits on the same policy as the drop trait, a `*_dup` is always settled by its `*_free`. **`CBox` is a sole owner; `CArc` shares.** `CBox::as_mut` hands out the exclusive handle, which is sound only while nothing else uses the object, so `CBox` clones only by deep copy. A refcounted object fits a `CBox` while the box holds its only reference (with the down-ref as `c_drop`); `CArc::from` shares it, and `CBox::try_from` (or `try_into_box`) takes it back once the count is 1 again. **Shared and mutable means locked — usually, part of it.** A `CArc` has no unlocked write path: its exclusive handle needs the count to prove the reference sole (`get_mut`, which needs `c_is_sole_owner` — an Acquire read of a count that covers every reference, C's own included), or a private copy (`make_mut`, through `CDupClone` — never a byte copy, which would duplicate the object's sub-allocations, its count and its lock). A C object rarely locks all of itself: it locks the state its holders mutate — a cache, a list of backends — and leaves the rest fixed once set up. That is `Arc` with a `Mutex` field, not `Arc>`, and the handles split the same way: | State | Handle | Reached through | |-------|--------|-----------------| | fixed once shared; routines that lock internally | `FooRef` | `CArc::as_ref()`, always | | protected by the lock — reads too; routines that need it held | `FooLocked` | `CArc::lock()` → `CGuard::as_locked()` | | anything | `FooMut` | `CArc::get_mut()`, sole reference only | A getter for protected state never goes on `FooRef`: it would race with a writer holding the lock through another clone. `CGuarded`'s contract makes C take or require the same lock, and makes the layout type invariant in any lifetime the protected state can hold (as a `Mutex` field does), so a covariant `CArc` cannot shrink one. The lock must not be recursive: a second `lock` on the same thread blocks forever, or panics when the lock reports the self-deadlock (`EDEADLK`), rather than hand out a second `FooLocked`. A failing C lock call panics, as `std`'s locks do; there is no poisoning. An object whose lock covers all of it is `CGuardedAll` (`impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)`): its locked handle is `FooMut`, so it is reached only through a `CGuardedRef`, which has no unlocked path, and `CArc::lock` rejects it at compile time. **Routines are plain paths, type-checked.** Each macro calls the routine with a pointer of the exact C type; a routine for the wrong type does not compile. Where a call can fail — an up_ref, a lock — the routine either returns `()` or is bound with `ok = |r| r == 1` (whatever its success value is); a status code is never silently discarded, so `pthread_mutex_lock`'s `EDEADLK` becomes a panic rather than a second locked handle. A routine of any other shape — a destructor taking the slot (`ffi::foo_free(&mut p)`), an up_ref or a copy that answers through an out-parameter (`ffi::foo_dup(&mut out, p)`), a `void *` allocator free, extra arguments — goes behind a small `unsafe fn` adapter passed to the macro by path. The adapter is private, with a `# Safety` section of its own, and sits beside the policy it serves, where the crate keeps its unsafe code (its unsafe region, if it has one), as a hand-written impl would. Prefer it to a hand-written `unsafe impl CDrop` (or `CRefClone`, `CDupClone`): the macro keeps the impl's shape and its type check of the C pointer, and the adapter adds no public unsafe surface, only a private `unsafe fn` and the unsafe block calling the routine, which a hand-written impl holds too. Teardown is unconditional: a gate that suppresses it on some paths folds into the routine itself. **A layout type with a lifetime.** A layout type that carries a lifetime, `Blob<'r>` over an object that keeps its repository, whether `define_ctype!` declares it or it is written by hand, takes its policies from the macros: `impl_cdrop!`, `impl_crefclone!` and `impl_cdispose!` accept it with the lifetime spelled `'_`, which the impl header turns into a parameter, so one policy serves `Blob<'r>` for every `'r`. A named lifetime (`Blob<'r>`) is undeclared there and does not compile. ```rust,ignore impl_cdrop!(BlobFree, Blob<'_>, ffi::blob_free); // `blob_dup` answers through an out-parameter: an adapter gives it the shape. impl_crefclone!(BlobFree, Blob<'_>, blob_up_ref, ok = |r| r == 0); pub type BlobArc<'r> = CArc, BlobFree>; ``` Two macros take the lifetime named instead, in a list ahead of their arguments. `impl_cdupclone!`'s `c_dup` returns the type, and a `'_` there elides to `&self`'s lifetime rather than the parameter's; `impl_cguarded!` names the type in a struct and an associated type, where `'_` is not allowed. ```rust,ignore impl_cdupclone!(<'r> BlobFree, Blob<'r>, ffi::blob_copy); impl_cguarded!(<'r> Cache<'r>, CacheLocked, lock = ffi::cache_lock, unlock = ffi::cache_unlock); // CacheLocked<'a, 'r>, the handle a held lock grants ``` A layout type generic over a type, rather than a lifetime, has no elided form: all its policies are hand-written. [examples.md](examples.md#a-layout-type-with-a-lifetime--define_ctype-with-phantom) shows the whole wrapper. **Runtime-state policies.** When teardown needs a value chosen at the wrapping site (`list_pop_free(list, elem_free_fn)`, `pool_free(pool, p)`), write the policy by hand — a struct holding the state, implementing `CDrop` (and `CDupClone` + `Clone` to clone) — and hold the object in a `CBoxState`, which stores the policy beside the pointer. Adopt with `from_raw_with(ptr, ElemFree(f))` and release with `into_raw_with()`. `CBox`, `CArc` and `CStrBox` hold a stateless policy, so that each is the pointer it stands in for; one with state fails to build in them. A routine known at compile time needs no state: a unit-struct policy per routine names it. **Construction goes through the policy too.** Bind a constructor to the policy and the owner's type pairs allocation with teardown, just as it pairs `*_dup` with `*_free`. A safely built `CBox` was allocated by `P`, and `from_raw` is the only way around that, which is why it is `unsafe`. - `CNew` is a type's own zero-argument constructor (`frame_alloc`). Constructors that take arguments stay inherent functions on `Foo` returning a `CBox`, because a trait signature cannot carry their parameters. - `CAllocZeroed` asks for zero-filled storage and needs `Foo: CZeroable`. That marker means all-zero is a state every safe accessor, every safe wrapper and the paired teardown accept, not merely a valid Rust value. Leave it off a type whose C constructor sets non-zero defaults. - `CAlloc` gives uninitialised storage, which C fills through `as_c_ptr` and the caller promotes with `unsafe assume_init`. # C tables implemented in Rust

A C library often takes a **table**: a struct of function pointers it calls
into, each slot passed a pointer to the table itself, which the implementer
embeds at the start of a larger allocation holding its own state. libgit2's
`git_config_backend`, `git_odb_backend` and `git_writestream` are such tables;
so is any "C inheritance" base struct with a `free` slot. Rust implements one
with a trait, and ffibox supplies the rest: [`CTable<T, S>`](#the-primitive)
holds Rust state `S` behind the C table of the layout type `T`, and
[`impl_cvtable!`](#declaring-a-table) mints the slots. It is `Box<dyn Trait>`
handed to C: a data part and a table of functions over it, the table embedded
rather than pointed to.

The inbound counterpart, a table C implements held from Rust, needs nothing
new: it is a `CBox` under a policy whose release calls the table's `free`
slot (`impl_cdrop!` over a private adapter), and its slots are called
through its handles. A binding with one owner for both, as libgit2's write
streams have, adopts a surrendered `CTable` into it (see (b)).

The binding still writes what is specific to the table: each slot's body,
which turns C's arguments into Rust's, calls the trait, and turns the result
into C's status convention. ffibox supplies only what is the same for every
table: the layout, the recovery of the state from the table pointer, the
re-entry rule, the panic barrier, the release and the owner.

## Decisions

### (a) A generic owner, and a macro for the slots only

`CTable<T, S>` is ordinary generic code: its layout (`#[repr(C)]`, the C table
first, then the entry state, then `S`), the entry protocol, the release, and
the owner's methods are written once, checked by the compiler and run under
Miri. The binding writes no struct of its own, so the table cannot be placed
anywhere but at offset zero; a compile-time assertion keeps it there.

What generics cannot express is the slots: an `extern "C" fn` of the C
declaration's exact signature, with the table at whichever argument C passes
it. `impl_cvtable!` mints those, and nothing else: one trampoline per slot,
whose whole body is a call to `CTable::enter`, and the `CSlots<S>` impl
(`base` and `install`, a safe trait) that installs them. The
trampolines are local to `install`, which takes a token only `CTable` makes,
branded with that one borrow of the table and the impl's types, so a slot
cannot be named, let alone installed in another table or over another state
type: each slot reaches `S` only through the table it was installed in. That
removes the recovery `unsafe` from every slot.

What types cannot check is one `unsafe impl CVtable<S> for T {}` per table,
an item-less trait whose contract it is: that C passes each slot its table in
the argument marked `@` (types check that where the table's is the only
argument of its type, but not where C passes another table of that type too,
`cmp(ops *self, ops *other)`), and that no slot C calls is left NULL. The
binding writes that line out in the macro's input, and the macro emits it
with the binding's own `unsafe` and braces, so the binding's lints see it:
`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` rejects the invocation, and clippy's
`undocumented_unsafe_blocks` asks for its `SAFETY` comment. The rest of C's
contract with the table is stated where the table is handed to C.

The table starts from `CSlots::base`, which the binding writes out
(`base = …;`, with no default: `Default::default()`, every slot NULL, is
right only when every slot C calls unconditionally is declared), and
`install` sets the slots it implements. Safe code therefore chooses no slot:
a binding's safe handle method that calls a slot of the table never runs a
function a consumer put there. A table whose fields are set per instance, or
that a C routine initialises, is built with the `unsafe` `CTable::with_base`,
whose caller states the same of its base.

The alternative, a generic `CTable<T: Table>` with an `unsafe` trait per C
table and hand-written trampolines, is also supported, since `enter` and
`release` are public: a slot the macro cannot express (a release of another
shape) is written by hand on the same terms, with one `unsafe` block per
slot. A slot takes doc comments only: an attribute such as
`#[target_feature]` would add an obligation to calling it that C cannot see. The macro is preferred
because it ties every slot to its table and state by construction; it is kept
to what an `unsafe impl` written by hand would contain (G20).

### (b) Slots that hand out C memory, and the table's own owner

A slot that hands C an object, an entry, an iterator, a buffer, returns it
through the owner that object already has: the body builds the owner and
surrenders it into C's out-parameter with `into_c` / `into_raw`. A nested
table (an iterator, an entry with its own `free`) is another `CTable`,
surrendered the same way and released by its own `free` slot. Nothing new is
needed: surrendering is safe, writing C's out-parameter is the binding's
`unsafe`, as it is today.

The table itself is owned by `CTable<T, S>` while Rust holds it. It lends
the table's handles, `T::Ref` / `T::Mut`, as `CBox` does, so the binding's
methods on them (a `write` that calls the slot) work on a Rust table as on a
C one. Those handles are the binding's, `Send` or `Sync` as the binding
decided for the C type, not for `S`; since their methods may call any slot,
`as_ref` and `as_mut` ask `S: Send + Sync`, as a `&RwLock<S>` shared between
threads does. Where the handles stay on their thread, as `define_ctype!`'s
do unless the binding opts in, the binding says so once per type with
`impl_clocal_handles!(T)`, which checks at compile time that neither handle
is `Send` or `Sync` before it implements `CLocalHandles`, and
`as_ref_local` / `as_mut_local` lend them, safely, over any `S`. `into_c` surrenders the table to C, which
releases it through the slot declared `release`. C keeps it past any borrow
and may use it on any thread, so `into_c` asks `S: Send + Sync + 'static`,
as `CPayload::into_raw` asks `Send + Sync`; the `unsafe` `into_c_local` asks
only `'static`, its caller stating the threads C uses. Where the binding has one owner for every table of that
type, C's and Rust's alike (`CBox<WriteStream, WriteStreamFree>`, whose
policy calls the `free` slot), the surrendered pointer is adopted into it with
`from_c`, `unsafe` as every adoption is: its obligation is that the policy
releases through the `free` slot. ffibox does not add a trait for that
obligation, which is one block per table type.

### (c) Receivers and re-entry

A slot declares its receiver in its body's argument type: `|s: &S|` is a
**shared** slot, `|s: &mut S|` an **exclusive** one, inferred by `enter`
from the closure, so a slot cannot get a receiver it did not declare. The
entry state is a non-blocking read-write lock over `S`, as
`RwLock::try_read` / `try_write` are:

- any number of shared slots run at once, re-entrant or on several threads;
- an exclusive slot runs only when no other slot does;
- a slot that cannot enter, an exclusive one while another slot runs or a
  shared one while an exclusive one does, is **refused**: it returns the value
  it declares `on busy`, without reaching `S`.

So re-entry is declared per slot, by its receiver, and a table whose slots
all take `&S` is never refused. The owner's own accessors take part:
`state(&self)` lends `&S` and refuses exclusive slots until the owner is next
borrowed mutably (it cannot see when the `&S` ends, so it waits for the
`&mut self` that proves it has); `state_mut` and `as_mut` take `&mut self`.

Release follows the same state. C's `free` while a slot runs, re-entrantly
from inside it or on another thread, is deferred: the slot that exits last
frees the allocation, on its own thread, and every slot entered while the
drop is deferred is refused. A `free` C calls on a table the owner still
holds is deferred to the owner's drop, and forgotten if the owner then
surrenders the table to C, which holds it anew. Each allocation is dropped
exactly once, whichever order C and Rust release it in.

### (d) Panics

Every trampoline runs its body in `callback::barrier`, and a slot declares
what a panic returns `on panic`, as it declares `on busy`: an error code, a
NULL, or `std::process::abort()` for a slot whose C convention cannot fail.
There is no default, so no two bindings of one convention disagree by
omission. Without `std` there is no barrier, and a panic aborts at the
`extern "C"` boundary. The `release` slot has no result: a panic in `S`'s
drop there aborts, as `CPayload::release_fn`'s does. A slot is not poisoned
by a panic: later calls run, and `S` is left as the unwinding left it, as
after any `barrier`.

---
name: toolchain
description: "Toolchains, edition, manifests, lints, formatting and unsafe-code rules of the generated workspace. Read before scaffolding the workspace or when a lint, format or toolchain question comes up."
---

# Rust

How the Rust a campaign generates is built, linted and formatted: its toolchains, its
edition, the lints every crate inherits and how it is formatted. What the code is named and
where it sits is [`conventions`](../conventions/SKILL.md)'s; these are the rules the toolchain
enforces on it.

## 1. Toolchains

The workspace builds and tests on stable Rust, pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml` to the
stable release current when the repository is created, with the `clippy` and `rustfmt`
components. Miri, the sanitizer and coverage instrumentation of the Rust,
BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain aside, and the formatter's unstable options need
nightly: a nightly pinned by date, recorded in the workspace manifest as
`[workspace.metadata.crustify] nightly = "nightly-<date>"`, and named explicitly wherever it
runs. A toolchain is moved forward only between waves, in a
commit of its own.

## 2. Edition and manifests

Every crate uses Rust edition 2024, with the workspace's `rust-version` set to the pinned
stable release. The shared package fields (`edition`, `rust-version`, `license`,
`repository`) are declared once, in `[workspace.package]`, and inherited. Every crate
inherits the workspace's lints with `[lints] workspace = true`.

## 3. Lints

The workspace declares its lints in `[workspace.lints.rust]` and `[workspace.lints.clippy]`.
Every gate runs with warnings denied, so a lint at `warn` fails a landing as surely as one
at `deny`; `deny` marks the lints no item may opt out of.

### 3.1 rustc

| lint | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `nonstandard_style` (`non_snake_case`, `non_camel_case_types`, `non_upper_case_globals`) | `deny` | the naming the conventions' Naming section gives: `snake_case` functions, methods, modules and variables, `UpperCamelCase` types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` constants and statics |
| `unsafe_code` | `warn` | unsafe code only in a module's unsafe regions, which take it back, as [Unsafe code](#5-unsafe-code) describes |
| `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` | `deny` | each unsafe operation in an `unsafe fn` sits in its own justified `unsafe` block |
| `missing_docs` | `warn` | every public item carries its anchor, which is a doc comment |
| `rust_2018_idioms` | `warn` | elided lifetimes in paths and other pre-2018 idioms |
| `unreachable_pub`, `unused_qualifications`, `unused_lifetimes`, `let_underscore_drop`, `trivial_casts`, `trivial_numeric_casts` | `warn` | visibility the crate does not need, and casts and drops that hide intent at the foreign boundary |

### 3.2 Clippy

| lints | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `clippy::correctness` | `deny` | code that is outright wrong |
| `clippy::all` (`suspicious`, `style`, `complexity`, `perf`), `clippy::pedantic`, `clippy::cargo` | `warn` | as much of Clippy's stable guidance as applies; `nursery` is left out, its lints still being unsettled |
| `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block`, `missing_safety_doc`, `unnecessary_safety_comment`, `unnecessary_safety_doc` | `deny` | every `unsafe` block is one justified operation, and every safety comment and `# Safety` section is where it belongs |
| `mem_forget`, `allow_attributes`, `allow_attributes_without_reason` | `deny` | no leak by `mem::forget`, and every exception an `#[expect]` with a reason |
| `module_inception` | `allow` | a C directory often holds a TU of its own name, so the mirrored tree nests a module in one of its name |
| `module_name_repetitions` | `allow` | items keep their C-derived names where their module, mirrored from the C path, repeats them |
| `multiple_crate_versions` | `allow` | the dependency graph is not the campaign's to dedupe |

An item that needs an exception takes it locally, as
`#[expect(<lint>, reason = "<why>")]`, never as a crate-wide `allow`: the expectation fails
once the exception is no longer needed.

### 3.3 Generated code

The raw bindings' bindgen output follows C's names and shapes, so it is exempt from the
workspace's lints: `src/sys.rs` allows every lint and lint group the workspace sets over
each generated module, under one `#[expect(clippy::allow_attributes, reason = "…")]`
naming the generated code, and the formatter skips the generated modules. The
hand-written parts of the raw bindings, such as `build.rs`, `src/sys.rs` itself and the
macro shims, follow the rest of this spec.

## 4. Formatting

Every crate is formatted by `rustfmt`, configured once in the workspace's `rustfmt.toml`:

| option | value |
|---|---|
| `edition`, `style_edition` | `"2024"` |
| `max_width`, `comment_width` | `100` |
| `newline_style` | `"Unix"` |
| `use_field_init_shorthand`, `use_try_shorthand` | `true` |
| `imports_granularity` | `"Module"` |
| `group_imports` | `"StdExternalCrate"` |
| `wrap_comments`, `normalize_comments`, `normalize_doc_attributes` | `true` |
| `format_code_in_doc_comments`, `format_macro_matchers` | `true` |
| `hex_literal_case` | `"Upper"` |
| `reorder_impl_items` | `true` |

The options from `imports_granularity` down are unstable, so the formatter runs on the

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
    > <file>.json
```

yet switched, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Export features section
names them, so that the `ffi_export` gateways compiled under them are counted. Every scan
names the module's unsafe regions, as the conventions' Unsafe regions section names them,
with `--regions`.

increments are, and takes leaves only, such as `fn.unsafe.pub`; the workspace is named

  `fn.unsafe.of_which.other.pub` are those neither a trait nor a seam required; and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, the raw pointers in

- `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`, the
  raw pointers in public fields and in the signatures of public safe fns, together

  `of_which.void` shares, the type-erased ones among them;

that belongs to the batch's changeset and that a safe variant could replace is fixed.

The audit's worksets are planned from a scan of the crate, run once each build
configuration it audits is in place, with `--sites` over the counters of its objectives.
A file outside every configuration scanned has no sites, and is planned from its source.

# Rust

How the Rust a campaign generates is built, linted and formatted: its toolchains, its
edition, the lints every crate inherits and how it is formatted. What the code is named and
where it sits is [`conventions`](../conventions/SKILL.md)'s; these are the rules the toolchain
enforces on it.

## 1. Toolchains

The workspace builds and tests on stable Rust, pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml` to the
stable release current when the repository is created, with the `clippy` and `rustfmt`
components. Miri, the sanitizer and coverage instrumentation of the Rust,
BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain aside, and the formatter's unstable options need
nightly: a nightly pinned by date, recorded in the workspace manifest as
`[workspace.metadata.crustify] nightly = "nightly-<date>"`, and named explicitly wherever it
runs. A toolchain is moved forward only between waves, in a
commit of its own.

## 2. Edition and manifests

Every crate uses Rust edition 2024, with the workspace's `rust-version` set to the pinned
stable release. The shared package fields (`edition`, `rust-version`, `license`,
`repository`) are declared once, in `[workspace.package]`, and inherited. Every crate
inherits the workspace's lints with `[lints] workspace = true`.

## 3. Lints

The workspace declares its lints in `[workspace.lints.rust]` and `[workspace.lints.clippy]`.
Every gate runs with warnings denied, so a lint at `warn` fails a landing as surely as one
at `deny`; `deny` marks the lints no item may opt out of.

### 3.1 rustc

| lint | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `nonstandard_style` (`non_snake_case`, `non_camel_case_types`, `non_upper_case_globals`) | `deny` | the naming the conventions' Naming section gives: `snake_case` functions, methods, modules and variables, `UpperCamelCase` types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` constants and statics |
| `unsafe_code` | `warn` | unsafe code only in a module's unsafe regions, which take it back, as [Unsafe code](#5-unsafe-code) describes |
| `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` | `deny` | each unsafe operation in an `unsafe fn` sits in its own justified `unsafe` block |
| `missing_docs` | `warn` | every public item carries its anchor, which is a doc comment |
| `rust_2018_idioms` | `warn` | elided lifetimes in paths and other pre-2018 idioms |
| `unreachable_pub`, `unused_qualifications`, `unused_lifetimes`, `let_underscore_drop`, `trivial_casts`, `trivial_numeric_casts` | `warn` | visibility the crate does not need, and casts and drops that hide intent at the foreign boundary |

### 3.2 Clippy

| lints | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `clippy::correctness` | `deny` | code that is outright wrong |
| `clippy::all` (`suspicious`, `style`, `complexity`, `perf`), `clippy::pedantic`, `clippy::cargo` | `warn` | as much of Clippy's stable guidance as applies; `nursery` is left out, its lints still being unsettled |
| `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block`, `missing_safety_doc`, `unnecessary_safety_comment`, `unnecessary_safety_doc` | `deny` | every `unsafe` block is one justified operation, and every safety comment and `# Safety` section is where it belongs |

| `module_inception` | `allow` | a C directory often holds a TU of its own name, so the mirrored tree nests a module in one of its name |
| `module_name_repetitions` | `allow` | items keep their C-derived names where their module, mirrored from the C path, repeats them |
| `multiple_crate_versions` | `allow` | the dependency graph is not the campaign's to dedupe |

An item that needs an exception takes it locally, as
`#[expect(<lint>, reason = "<why>")]`, never as a crate-wide `allow`: the expectation fails
once the exception is no longer needed.

The raw bindings' bindgen output follows C's names and shapes, so it is exempt from the
workspace's lints: `src/sys.rs` allows every lint and lint group the workspace sets over
each generated module, under one `#[expect(clippy::allow_attributes, reason = "…")]`
naming the generated code, and the formatter skips the generated modules. The
hand-written parts of the raw bindings, such as `build.rs`, `src/sys.rs` itself and the
macro shims, follow the rest of this spec.

Every crate is formatted by `rustfmt`, configured once in the workspace's `rustfmt.toml`:

| option | value |
|---|---|
| `edition`, `style_edition` | `"2024"` |
| `max_width`, `comment_width` | `100` |
| `newline_style` | `"Unix"` |
| `use_field_init_shorthand`, `use_try_shorthand` | `true` |
| `imports_granularity` | `"Module"` |
| `group_imports` | `"StdExternalCrate"` |
| `wrap_comments`, `normalize_comments`, `normalize_doc_attributes` | `true` |
| `format_code_in_doc_comments`, `format_macro_matchers` | `true` |
| `hex_literal_case` | `"Upper"` |
| `reorder_impl_items` | `true` |

pinned nightly. A landing's tree is formatted, and the gate checks that it is.
